papers.title: Automated, auditable dating of the Babylonian Astronomical Diaries with language models and astronomical tools
papers.abstract: The Babylonian Astronomical Diaries record the sky over nearly six centuries. Many tablets are broken and have lost their date formula. Experts dated many of them one tablet at a time in the standard edition, Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia (ADART). They used the recorded sky and other evidence, such as year formulas and royal names. Our system automates the astronomical part for all tablets with the same rules. A rule-based parser turns the recorded observations into clauses, short statements with fixed fields. A language model checks them against the text and adds observations that the parser missed. Astronomical tools test the clauses in all 701 years from 626 BCE to AD 75. The system ranks the years by how well they agree with the clauses. The system withholds published dates until its results are final, and the output lists the passages and computed positions behind each candidate year. On 120 dated tablets, the years tied at the top of the ranking include the published year in 96% of cases. For 86 of them, this top group is a single year, the published year in 84. In 119 of the 120, the reported candidate set contains it. For 56 undated entries of ADART IV, the system gives ranked candidate years. For each tablet, the results show how far astronomy alone narrows the year. An interactive page at https://tingyuansen.github.io/Babylonian_Dating/ follows each tablet and links the code, protocol and results.

papers.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
papers.abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80{\deg}S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.

papers.title: Machine Learning Applications in the Solar Interior and Atmosphere
papers.abstract: The solar interior and atmosphere constitute a strongly coupled, multiscale dynamical system defined by continuous temporal evolution. Predicting the state of this system requires modeling physical interactions that span disparate spatial and temporal scales, constrained by heterogeneous and sparse data. This chapter formalizes the Sun within the mathematical framework of dynamical systems theory, defining a global state vector ($\vec{S}$) governed by thermodynamical, kinetic, and magnetic properties. Because solar observations represent projected, multi-modal, and partially observable measurements ($\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$) of this hidden state, pure physics-based deduction is fundamentally constrained. We present a unifying thesis: the primary role of machine learning in heliophysics is to act as a structured family of mathematical operators---specifically Inference ($\mathcal{I}$), Emulation ($\mathcal{E}$), Propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and Control ($\mathcal{C}$)---that reconstruct, simulate, and couple this global state vector across disparate physical layers. By framing the vast, multi-disciplinary literature within this unified state-space taxonomy, we demonstrate how data-driven techniques bridge observational gaps to resolve hidden multiscale couplings and dramatically accelerate the simulation of non-linear processes, establishing a rigorous pathway to predict the global evolution of the Sun.

papers.title: FastPM: Fast Pretrained Model for Cosmological Simulation-Based Inference
papers.abstract: Modern cosmology increasingly relies on large ensembles of expensive simulations to model the non-linear Universe and extract information from upcoming surveys. However, generating high-fidelity simulations---whether gravity-only N-body or full hydrodynamical---requires substantial computational resources. In this work, we demonstrate that transfer learning from fast low-fidelity simulations can dramatically reduce the cost of training machine learning models, in particular for simulation-based inference (SBI). We train a Fast Pretrained Model (FastPM) on a set of Fast Particle-Mesh (FastPM) simulations to infer $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ from the power spectrum, and finetune on a smaller set of high-fidelity CAMELS N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. To reach a fixed posterior accuracy, the pretrained model requires only 5--15\% of the high-fidelity simulations compared to the number of simulations needed when training on CAMELS alone, reducing the total training simulation compute cost, including that of the pretraining simulations, by up to an order of magnitude in CPU hours. Remarkably, the gains persist for the total matter power spectrum of full hydrodynamical simulations: although FastPM contains no baryonic physics, pretraining on FastPM runs that together cost less than a single hydrodynamical simulation still reduces the total training simulation compute by a factor of $\sim$5. Moreover, pretraining on more accurate FastPM runs yields more accurate posteriors than training on CAMELS alone achieves with any number of simulations we consider. These results demonstrate that transfer learning from fast simulations is a simple and powerful route to high-fidelity SBI, and highlight the promise of simulation-based foundation models in cosmology.

papers.title: Calibration requirements for Epoch of Reionization 21-cm signal observations - V. Bias and variance in the cylindrical power spectrum from uGMRT Band 3 observations of the ELAIS-N1 field
papers.abstract: Detection of the redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen requires precise control of systematic effects arising from instrumental calibration. In this work, we investigate the impact of both time- and frequency-dependent residual gain and bandpass errors on the estimation of the multifrequency angular power spectrum (MAPS) using radio interferometric observations. We discuss our previously developed analytical framework for estimating bias and excess variance in 21-cm signal MAPS in the presence of these residual errors and apply it to uGMRT Band-3 observations. The statistical properties of the residual gains are derived from the data themselves, including their temporal and spectral correlations. We introduce a robust technique for additionally flagging poor-quality data. Our results show that the excess variance induced by residual gain and bandpass errors dominates over the bias across the range of angular multipoles considered. The amplitude of this variance is comparable to the expected power spectrum upper limit at redshift $z \sim 2.2$, indicating that residual calibration errors can significantly affect the detectability of the 21-cm signal. We further transform the estimated MAPS into ($k_{\perp}, k_{ll}$) space and find the expected foreground wedge structure. Importantly, we observe a significant power leakage into the nominal EoR window, which we attribute to residual calibration systematics. This highlights that even after standard foreground mitigation, time- and frequency-correlated gain errors can introduce mode-mixing and contaminate the EoR window. Our results emphasise the necessity of improved calibration accuracy and robust characterisation of residual gain statistics for current and upcoming interferometric experiments such as the uGMRT and SKA, to enable reliable detection of the cosmological 21-cm signal.

papers.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
papers.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $\mu $s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

papers.title: Identifying Cosmic Ray Over-Flagging in STIS CCD Spectroscopic Observations
papers.abstract: The standard method for rejecting cosmic rays in CCD data taken by the Hubble Space Telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) instrument relies on combining multiple sub-exposures while flagging outliers. A known caveat of this method is that when the sub-exposures are not well registered, large portions of valid spectroscopic data can be flagged as cosmic rays. In this work we discuss the new ocrreject_exam() task in the stistools Python package designed to quickly identify datasets impacted by this misregistration-induced over-flagging. We demonstrate its effectiveness on known cases of over-flagged data, introduce a new monitoring website which automatically runs the tool on STIS CCD spectroscopic data, and analyze the tool's output on STIS CCD spectroscopic data from 1997 through 2025. From this analysis we estimate that ~31% of datasets will exhibit cosmic ray over-flagging. Lastly, we discuss various methods of recalibrating impacted data to mitigate the effects of over-flagging.

papers.title: Faint Companions to Hot Stars. Spectroscopic Detection Sensitivity and Implications for Survey Design
papers.abstract: Searches for black holes in binaries must distinguish dark companions from faint luminous stars. This is challenging for hot stars, whose spectra contain few broad lines. We develop a Fourier-domain method that converts isolated, broadened lines into calibrated constraints on faint companions. Doppler shifts are encoded in the Fourier phase, while the line profile defines a smooth amplitude envelope. A faint secondary introduces an oscillatory perturbation to the log-amplitude. Expanding to first order in the secondary-to-primary line-depth ratio, $\alpha$, yields a nearly linear model for a likelihood-ratio test against the single-star model. The method applies to single or multiple epochs without full spectral disentangling. At small velocity separation $v$, the companion signal becomes degenerate with the primary line profile, and the fractional uncertainty from the log-amplitude scales as $\Delta\alpha/\alpha \propto v^{-4}$. If the primary velocity is known, the Fourier phase provides a more favorable detection channel whose sensitivity scales as $v^{-1}$. We demonstrate the method on archival FEROS spectra of CPD$-41^\circ$7742, detecting the known secondary in He I 6678 Angstrom and obtaining a stringent non-detection in He II 5411 Angstrom, where its contribution is expected to be negligible. The framework yields detection efficiencies as functions of line-depth ratio, velocity separation, noise, and instrumental setup. These can be combined across lines, epochs, and targets to construct selection functions for spectroscopic black-hole searches, including those enabled by SDSS-V and Gaia.

papers.title: O Mirror, Where Art Thou?
papers.abstract: Wavefront sensing reveals that a telescope is misaligned, but not which mirror moved or by how much; inferring the mirror positions themselves turns alignment into a direct correction. We describe a simulation framework for inferring telescope mirror misalignment from multi-field Point Spread Function (PSF) measurements projected onto Circular-Bessel and Zernike basis vectors. Two case studies are presented: a Hubble Space Telescope model with five secondary-mirror degrees of freedom and a three-mirror anastigmat with ten primary and secondary mirror degrees of freedom. In both cases, field-dependent multivariate Gaussian likelihoods are explored with nested sampling and refined with differential evolution. Recovered states are validated with residual PSF images and optical path difference (OPD) measurements. In the Hubble benchmark, differential evolution recovers injected misalignments to less than 0.01 microns and reduces on-axis OPD error from 2.3 waves to 3 x 10E-8 waves. In the TMA study, the posterior shows broad marginals and correlated parameter pairs that suggest partial degeneracies at higher dimension; differential evolution recovers the truth alignment state less precisely than in the Hubble benchmark (less than 17 microns) and reduces on-axis OPD error from 8.24 waves to 2 x 10E-3 waves. This generalizable algorithm enables direct sensing of the state of an optical system and automated alignment.

papers.title: Atmospheric Turbulence Profiling in the Lenghu Site Area Using MERRA-2 Data
papers.abstract: The Lenghu site, in the Saishiteng Mountains of the northern Tibetan Plateau, has been identified as an excellent astronomical site from preliminary statistics of clear nights, sky background brightness, precipitable water vapour, total seeing and weather. Since 2022, several projects with apertures larger than 4 m have started construction or are being planned. Given the use of adaptive optics (AO) on these projects, in-depth measurements and analysis of the atmospheric turbulence above the site are required: the distribution and variation of the turbulence profiles provide a large-scale, climatological basis for site planning and for comparing candidate locations, complementing rather than replacing the on-site measurements needed for instrument design and operations. Predicting the atmospheric profiles of the site and its surroundings from satellite data, combined with on-site measurements, can help to optimise the site planning. This paper uses MERRA-2 reanalysis data to study the atmospheric profiles of the site and its environment, revealing the seasonal and long-term variations of the observing conditions. The reanalysis results are cross-checked against on-site ground-level instruments serving the same purpose. MERRA-2 overestimates the median free-atmosphere seeing by +0.22 arcsec (+50 %) while keeping the night-to-night correlation weak (r ~ 0.2), and underestimates the median total seeing by -0.24 arcsec (-27 %). It captures only ~22 % of the ground-layer turbulence and little of the observed seasonal amplitude of the free atmosphere. MERRA-2 is therefore suited to relative comparisons of spatial variability between locations and to climatological characterisation, not to quantitative AO applications or night-by-night assessment of profiles.

papers.title: ePNGCAT: the first eROSITA all-sky data release
papers.abstract: The eROSITA telescope array aboard the joint German--Russian Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission delivered the deepest soft all-sky X-ray survey to date, scanning the entire sky more than four times between December 2019 and February 2022. The potential of the survey remains, however, hampered by the fact that only data for the half of the sky owned by the German consortium have been released publicly, whereas the other half remains accessible only to the Russian consortium, effectively making eROSITA a "half-sky" survey for most applications. The only publicly accessible all-sky "data product" as of 2026 is a single press-release image published in June 2020 jointly by both consortia to celebrate the completion of the first all-sky survey (eRASS1). Here I present the first all-sky eROSITA catalogue based on this image, containing around 63 thousand sources with an estimated completeness of about 50% above $3\times10^{-13}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ in the 0.2-2.3 keV band and a positional accuracy of $\sim$1 arcmin, validated against the full eRASS1 catalogue for half the sky and against several external catalogues. The catalogue is thus comparable with 2RXS, the deepest truly all-sky survey generally available, and gives a first glimpse of the eastern Galactic hemisphere with eROSITA. In this hemisphere, about 11000 detected sources have no counterpart in ROSAT or other public X-ray catalogues and are expected to be genuine new X-ray sources. Besides the catalogue, I release calibrated HEALPix maps to facilitate studies of large-scale extended emission, such as the eROSITA bubbles, or of Galactic absorption that require full sky coverage (https://zenodo.org/records/23640281), as well as the complete analysis pipeline to make the results fully reproducible (https://github.com/doroshv/eropngcat).

papers.title: Magnetic Topological Evolution and the Predictive Role of Winding-flux-based Masked PILs in Extreme Solar Flares from AR13664 and AR13842
papers.abstract: Using vector magnetogram data from the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager (HMI) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we present detailed case studies of precursor activity in Active Regions (ARs) 13664 and 13842, which produced several intense flares. We examined the spatiotemporal evolution of key magnetic topological parameters, including winding, helicity, winding-flux-based masked polarity inversion lines (PILs), and PIL gradients, from the precursor to the post-flare phases. The temporal evolution of the winding flux showed a significant enhancement during the precursor phase, and this trend was consistent across the seven X-class and five M-class flares (>= M5.0). The spatial distribution of both raw and Gaussian-smoothed winding-flux enhancement is co-located with flare footpoint regions of highly twisted core fields, as indicated by the photospheric magnetic topology. The winding-flux-based masked PILs that persisted around the flare locations showed a significant increase in strength and area during the precursor activity. These masked PILs spatially coincide with regions likely hosting non-potential core magnetic fields associated with the observed flares. Furthermore, the gradient of strong PILs extracted from the ARs was positively correlated with flare-associated locations and typically increased several hours (approx. 3-5 h) before flare onset. By imposing a gradient threshold on strong PILs, we isolate magnetic regions repeatedly associated with flare initiation, providing useful constraints in regimes where current flare-forecasting models remain uncertain. Therefore, the combined analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution of different magnetic topological parameters enhances our understanding of intense solar flare forecasting and the identification of potential triggering sites, thereby contributing to improved space weather prediction frameworks.

papers.title: Reproducibility, Methodological Robustness, and Synthetic-Domain Selection Properties of AFINO for TESS Stellar-Flare QPP Analysis
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pulsation (QPP) searches in stellar flares depend on methodological choices that can affect both classification and the interpretation of recovered periods. A defensible assessment therefore requires explicit separation of reproducibility, robustness, and known-truth performance. We characterize the reproducibility, methodological robustness, numerical behavior, and synthetic-ground-truth selection properties of a frozen public AFINO implementation in the TESS context while keeping observational reference evidence separate from known synthetic truth. The frozen baseline reproduced five published TESS detections in the initial reproduction cohort. A ten-event observational pilot and a catalogue-scale robustness experiment then tested prospectively specified temporal-window and processing perturbations. At catalogue scale, 51 of 61 published-QPP references did not reproduce their frozen reference state under the F3A baseline, so robustness claims were conditioned on baseline-concordant references rather than interpreted as accuracy. In a separately developed synthetic programme, the untouched AFINO 0.5 rule was evaluated once on an independent HELDOUT set: 152 of 1800 synthetic positives were selected and no false selections were observed among 1800 synthetic nulls, with finite Wilson uncertainty. The resulting 156-stratum selection surface and period-recovery summaries remain conditional on the frozen synthetic domain and, for period recovery, on selection; they therefore provide a bounded characterization of methodological robustness and synthetic-domain selection behavior without establishing observational validation or a population-level correction.

papers.title: Data-driven acquisition offset correction for telescope networks using machine learning and sensitivity analysis
papers.abstract: Reliable target acquisition is essential for maximizing observing efficiency, particularly for robotic telescope networks that operate across many sites, instruments, and environmental conditions. Although these facilities generate large volumes of operational and observational data, acquisition procedures often continue to rely on static pointing models and manual adjustments by observatory staff. These approaches can be effective, but they may not fully capture changing behavior associated with telescope configuration, observing conditions, instrument state, or other time-dependent effects. We present a data-driven machine-learning pipeline for automatically predicting and correcting telescope acquisition offsets, demonstrated using archival operational logs from the Las Cumbres Observatory network. Our approach applies both traditional machine-learning methods and deep-learning regression models to learn relationships between measured acquisition offsets and a range of observing, telescope, and instrumentation conditions. By using historical performance data, the pipeline is designed to complement existing pointing models and reduce the need for repeated manual correction. We also present an open-source, Dockerized software service that makes the trained models accessible through a browser-based graphical interface. The service is intended to support straightforward, real-time use by observatory staff while remaining portable across computing environments. Together, the prediction pipeline and deployment framework provide a practical path toward more adaptive, automated, and data-informed telescope acquisition.

papers.title: Experimental Validation of Double-Blind Fourier Holography in an HWO-Like Segmented Aperture
papers.abstract: Double-Blind Fourier Holography (DBFH) is a phase-retrieval method that has been shown numerically to address wavefront-sensing challenges for future segmented-aperture space telescopes, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). DBFH uses a set of carefully selected pupil-plane amplitude masks and their corresponding focal-plane intensity measurements to construct an algebraically linear inverse problem, enabling computationally efficient and stable reconstruction of the complex pupil field. Here, we present the first experimental demonstration of DBFH using a spatial light modulator and an HWO EAC5-like segmented-aperture geometry. We reconstruct challenging pseudo-random wavefronts and compare DBFH with the established Focus-Diverse Phase Retrieval (FDPR) method. The two methods achieve comparable reconstruction precision, while exhibiting distinct strengths and limitations. We further demonstrate DBFH wavefront sensing in the presence of a binary source, a scenario that is not naturally accommodated by conventional FDPR. These results provide experimental proof of concept and establish technology readiness level 3 for DBFH as a wavefront-sensing method for space telescopes with segmented primary mirrors.

papers.title: A frequency-resolved measurement of the scattering law in FRB 20210415C
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) show diverse temporal morphologies, shaped both by their intrinsic emission and by propagation effects such as residual dispersion and multipath scattering. Because several of these effects can broaden a burst asymmetrically, an asymmetric profile does not by itself establish multipath scattering. We measure the frequency dependence of the temporal tail in FRB 20210415C, a bright burst from the repeating source FRB 20210219C. The burst is detected across approximately 400-800 MHz. Frequency-resolved fits yield an empirical exponential-tail timescale, $\tau_{\rm emp}$, that follows $\tau_{\rm emp}\propto\nu^{\alpha}$. Two complementary treatments of the underlying pulse width give $\alpha=-3.95\pm0.07$ and $-4.14\pm0.08$. Both results are consistent with the commonly adopted $\nu^{-4}$ scattering law. The inferred scattering time is approximately 8.0 ms at 583 MHz, exceeding Galactic foreground estimates by a factor of at least $4\times10^{2}$. This favours a dominant contribution beyond the Milky Way, although the data do not localise the scattering screen. FRB 20210415C therefore provides a direct measurement of a scattering law commonly imposed in catalogue analyses.

papers.title: Power spectrum of longitudinal-velocity residuals in the Galactic disk from Gaia DR3 red-giant-branch stars
papers.abstract: Non-axisymmetric structures in the Galaxy produce coherent stellar motions in the Galactic disk. These motions are usually interpreted by assuming parameterized gravitational potentials or specific perturbation models, thereby entangling direct kinematic information with model-dependent assumptions. Using Gaia DR3 astrometry, we analyze the Galactic longitudinal-velocity residuals of nearly four million red-giant-branch stars over $-4 < X_h < 4\, \mathrm{kpc}$ and $-6 < Y_h < 6\, \mathrm{kpc}$ in the heliocentric region. We construct an empirical axisymmetric baseline without introducing any dynamical model, and compute the power spectrum of the residual velocity field. The spectrum exhibits a broad peak at spatial frequency of $f \simeq 0.12 - 0.22\, \mathrm{kpc}^{-1}$, corresponding to a scale of around $5-8\, \mathrm{kpc}$. The residual amplitude is sensitive to the adopted distance scale: inverse-parallax distances $d_\varpi$ yield a peak of around $16\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$, while the Bailer-Jones geometric distances $r_{\mathrm{geo}}$ yield around $12\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$. Minimizing the low-frequency power favors a solar radial motion of $U_\odot=10.8\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$ based on $d_\varpi$ and $U_\odot=10.4\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$ based on $r_{\mathrm{geo}}$. Collectively, the resulting spectrum establishes Gaia astrometry as a direct probe of disk-wide non-axisymmetric kinematics and provides quantitative targets for future dynamical modeling and interpretation.

papers.title: GOWC: an open tool for observing-conditions prediction and observation planning, tested against site monitors and an exposure-time calculator
papers.abstract: GOWC (Global Observing-conditions Weather Catalogue) is an open web application that takes the user from a target to an exposure plan across 2,642 catalogued observatory sites. It computes seeing, airmass, extinction, precipitable water vapour, sky brightness and signal-to-noise from live Open-Meteo meteorology, including pressure-level profiles, and tests most of these outputs against an independent reference. The photometric SNR calculator, run with GOWC's own catalogue entries, reproduces the ING SIGNAL exposure-time calculator to a median 1.9 per cent over a 16-point magnitude-airmass grid on two instruments. Precipitable water vapour tracks the Paranal LHATPRO radiometer closely ($\rho=+0.95$, 606 nights) with a +43 per cent wet bias. Seeing is computed from the Tatarski $C_n^2$ chain integrated over the pressure levels above the site and calibrated to the ESO MASS free-atmosphere median at Paranal; matching it requires an effective Tatarski coefficient of 5.7, nearly twice the upper end of the published range, which quantifies how much turbulence four coarse pressure levels fail to resolve. Against ~20 months of ESO DIMM data the seeing forecast has a weak but significant night-to-night ranking skill ($\rho=+0.24$, 575 nights, at Paranal; +0.16 at La Silla). Surface wind alone does as well or better (+0.27, +0.41) and persistence does better (+0.42, +0.47), but the free-atmosphere term tracks MASS ($\rho=+0.35$) and carries information that surface wind does not (partial $\rho=+0.28$, +0.40). At held-out sites the absolute seeing scale is no better than a constant. GOWC therefore treats forecast seeing as indicative, shows measured values wherever a public site monitor exists, and states which outputs are measured, calibrated or unvalidated.

papers.title: Comparison of Hybrid and Standard Reconstruction Methods on IXPE Astrophysical Data
papers.abstract: The hybrid reconstruction algorithm developed by Cibrario et al. 2023 combined a convolutional neural network (CNN) with standard moment analysis to improve track reconstruction in IXPE Gas Pixel Detectors. Although validated on laboratory data (Cibrario et al. 2025), the method's astrophysical performance had not been systematically characterized. We present the first comparison of hybrid and standard reconstruction on IXPE point sources, measuring sensitivity gains versus energy. We analyze Her X-1, a bright, polarized accreting pulsar as a benchmark, and soft-state XTE J1701-461, a bright neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary with no detected polarization, to assess residual systematics. From both pipelines' Level-2 event files, we compare normalized Stokes parameters, polarization degree (PD) and angle (PA), and detection significance. For Her X-1, hybrid reconstruction increases significance at all energies, significantly above ~2.83 keV. R = {\sigma}_hyb/{\sigma}_std differs from unity by 9.3{\sigma} in the 2.83-4.00 keV bin and reaches 1.18\pm0.03 at 5.66-8.00 keV (6.2{\sigma}). For XTE J1701-461, PD is consistent with zero and R with unity. Fourier analysis reveals excess power in hybrid angle distributions at low energies for modes m = 3, 6, 12 and 15, significant at >7{\sigma} relative to the standard method; at 5-8 keV, all modes are consistent with noise in both methods. These CNN-amplified hexagonal-grid artifacts do not affect Stokes parameters because they are orthogonal to polarization modes.The method delivers a statistically significant sensitivity gain for Her X-1, consistent with Cibrario et al. 2025 and equivalent to ~20% more effective area without extra observing time. These results support systematic use of hybrid reconstruction on IXPE astrophysical data.

papers.title: SoFTg: A hybrid segmentation framework for solar granulation revealing turbulent convection statistics at DKIST scales
papers.abstract: In this work, we present Solar Feature Tracking: granules (SoFTg), a new hybrid algorithm within the SoFT library designed for the segmentation and tracking of solar granulation. By combining a heuristic approach based on a custom adaptive-thresholding technique with the speed and robustness of deep-learning methods, SoFTg provides a fast, reliable and user-friendly solution for granule segmentation, followed by the standard SoFT approach for tracking. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm's performance using multiple metrics and analyse the different stages of the processing pipeline. The method is tested on three datasets acquired with the Visible Broadband Imager operating in the red continuum at the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Maui, Hawaii. We present distributions of both the lifetime and equivalent diameter of the thousands of granules tracked, providing, for the first time, statistically robust evidence of turbulent convection at the spatial scales now accessible through the high-resolution imaging capabilities of DKIST.

papers.title: Space Electric and Magnetic Sensor (SEAMS) Phase I: A Pathfinder Mission for Low-Frequency Radio Astronomy
papers.abstract: In this paper, the Space Electric and Magnetic Sensor (SEAMS), a space based mission dedicated to very low frequency (below 16 MHz) observations of the radio sky is proposed. The SEAMS mission is planned in two phases. The first phase is specifically designed for radio frequency interference (RFI) mapping from the low earth orbit (LEO). The low frequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum is filled with a variety of artificial as well as natural RFI. Previous observations have confirmed the effect of this terrestrial interference on astronomical observations. Thus, a map of terrestrial RFI as observed from space would give valuable information to groups working in the low-frequency regime. For the first phase, the payload will be mounted on to the fourth stage of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)'s third generation Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), which will stay in LEO for several weeks. The payload consists of a pair of orthogonal active monopoles, a simple baseband sampling receiver optimized for recording power spectra from each antenna. The design also aims to detect strong signals of astronomical origin despite RFI. In the second phase, we intend to send a more sophisticated space payload to orbit the moon and subsequently land on its surface.

papers.title: A Congestion-Aware RDMA Front-End for LST Advanced Camera Readout
papers.abstract: The Advanced Camera (AdvCam) upgrade of the Large-Sized Telescopes (LSTs) calls for a fully digital readout in which each front-end board streams data to the event-building servers over commercial 10 Gb/s Ethernet, using an FPGA implementation of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Converged Ethernet v2 (RoCEv2). In a previous work, a customized RoCEv2 core integrated with the SLAC SURF UDP/MAC stack was shown to sustain near-line-rate data transfers from a Xilinx KCU105 to a server equipped with a Mellanox ConnectX-5 NIC. However, the AdvCam topology is an incast funnel: many 10 GbE links converge onto a single uplink, and bare Priority Flow Control (PFC) congestion management protocol is known to be unfair and to suffer from head-of-line blocking. This work extends the previous design with the Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification (DCQCN) algorithm. A protocol-level ns-3 simulation is used to validate the DCQCN dynamics and to explore the parameter space; an FPGA rate-limiter integrated into the SURF MAC reacts to incoming Congestion Notification Packets (CNPs) according to the DCQCN state machine; a cocotb testbench with an emulated Python switch verifies the firmware end-to-end against a Soft-RoCE receiver; and a three-sender incast hardware test on a DCQCN-enabled commercial switch reproduces the canonical fair-share, reactive-redistribution, and saw-tooth behaviour expected from a commercial RDMA NIC. The internal rate-limiter register is shown to track the measured RoCEv2 throughput cycle by cycle.

papers.title: The biases caused by interpolated table models and their impact on X-ray spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Models for X-ray spectroscopy involving complex relativistic or plasma physics are commonly pre-computed on a grid, In this paper, we aim to quantify the potential biases and distortions introduced by the computational error and propagated into parameter inference by interpolating linearly these complex, non-linear models. We analyse the performance of Bayesian sampling algorithms on mock inference problems. Then, we model real observations of an accreting black hole X-ray binary in both the soft and hard states. We find that linear interpolation can a) greatly bias the posterior distribution of model parameters and b) distort the likelihood space to such a degree that posterior distributions become artificially multimodal. This multi-modality causes a noticeable loss in computational efficiency in both sampling and fitting techniques. As a result, exploring a given parameter space until convergence requires an extremely large computational cost. These findings call for improving the computational techniques used when fitting modern X-ray data, for example through better sampling algorithms and/or more sophisticated interpolation schemes

papers.title: The design and flight of the Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO)
papers.abstract: Sources of cosmic rays at ultrahigh energies (UHE, $\gtrsim$ 1 EeV) are anticipated to give rise to neutrinos at similar energies by production via propagation interactions either within the source region or on cosmological scales. Measurements of the neutrino flux, flavor, and energy provide significant insight into those underlying processes governing UHE cosmic ray acceleration and propagation. Detecting neutrinos at these energies requires immense detector volumes due to their low predicted flux. We present the balloon-borne mission PUEO (Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations) which is an antenna array designed to detect the Askaryan emission from UHE neutrino interactions in the Antarctic ice. This paper reports on the design considerations and implementations for constructing PUEO, from the design parameters to the as-built validations.

papers.title: Spectroscopic Survey of Small Solar System Bodies with Ariel
papers.abstract: The small Solar System bodies (SSSBs) preserve records of the formation and evolution of the Solar System. In particular, the near-infrared wavelength region around 3 $\mu$m provides crucial insights into the origin and transport of hydrated materials and organics, although it is difficult to observe from the ground because of strong telluric absorption. We assess the observability of SSSBs as complementary science to the ESA Ariel space mission, operating in the visible to mid-infrared wavelength range (0.5--7.8 $\mu$m). Using the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system, we evaluate the visibility of known SSSBs from 2032 to 2035. Our analysis shows that Ariel can spectroscopically characterize up to 402 unique SSSBs under a conservative limiting visual magnitude of $V=13.6$. If observations can be extended to somewhat fainter targets ($V=16$), the number of observable SSSBs could increase to 2144. Assuming operational scenarios in which one SSSB is observed every 3, 7, or 30 days over a four-year mission, the total numbers of observable targets would be 357, 209, and 49, respectively. We further model the spectral energy distributions of candidate targets to evaluate their observational performance. We demonstrate that Ariel can resolve critical absorption features, such as those at 2.7 $\mu$m and 3.4 $\mu$m, with a higher spectral resolution than the previous infrared survey with AKARI. Observations of SSSBs with Ariel can provide insights into the distribution and evolution of life-forming materials in the Solar System and constitute a scientifically compelling component of Ariel's complementary science program.

papers.title: Accurate pulsar timing array likelihoods: better low-rank covariance for gravitational wave background
papers.abstract: In pulsar timing array analyses, the stochastic process describing the gravitational wave background is typically modeled using a Fourier basis at discrete frequencies with an interval $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, with a diagonal Fourier-domain covariance determined by the power spectral density at the corresponding frequencies. Although this rank-reduced modeling significantly accelerates likelihood evaluation and provides a good approximation in many scenarios, it can lead to biased parameter inference because it is insensitive to spectral features on scales smaller than $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. We introduce a better construction of the low-rank covariance for low-frequency processes by maximizing the log-likelihood averaged over an ensemble of realizations drawn from the true model likelihood. In this approach, the basis-domain covariance matrix is sensitive to the entire model spectrum and is generally non-diagonal. Using two mock datasets, we demonstrate improved likelihood accuracy and more faithful recovery of spectral features compared to the conventional Fourier-diagonal model. Benchmark tests show that this new model requires a computational cost comparable to that of the conventional approach.

papers.title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation
papers.abstract: We developed an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large- area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for the NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful integration of the DAQ system.

papers.title: Near-exact Upper Confidence Limits for Axion Haloscopes
papers.abstract: The data acquisition of axion haloscopes commonly implements sequential adaptive frequency scans. We present a method to calculate likelihood-based upper confidence limits on axion-photon coupling under this circumstance. We compare the likelihood-based method conceptually and quantitatively with tailor-made methods, i.e. the one proposed by Brubaker et al. (Geometric) and its upgrade the Bayesian Power-Measured (BPM) framework proposed by Palken et al. We find that the likelihood method yields average upper limits that are significantly more constraining than those obtained from these methods. For example, expected constraints improve by a factor of 1.4 as compared with the current state of the art when applied to projections for the ALPHA Plasma-haloscope. We further clarify the statistical basis for the Geometric and BPM methods. In particular, we point out the correspondence of BPM to e-values, proposed as an alternative to conventional p-values in statistics.

papers.title: NRHJSur3dq8: a spectral numerical-relativity surrogate family for non-eccentric aligned-spin binary-black-hole waveforms
papers.abstract: We present NRHJSur3dq8, a family of numerical-relativity surrogates for non-eccentric aligned-spin binary-black-hole waveforms inspired by an action-angle parameterization. The model provides both the dynamics: the Hamiltonian values, azimuthal action $J_\phi(\Phi)$, the orbital clock $\tau(\Phi)$ as functions of its phasing, and the radiative pieces: the waveforms, their near-analytic derivatives, and modeling errors associated with each. The surrogated variables are conditioned into pieces that vary slowly on the radiation-reaction timescale, represented on shared $h$-adaptive Chebyshev elements, and regressed across the intrinsic parameters with a Gaussian-process model. A time-parameterized merger-ringdown set of elements is attached where the adiabatic description breaks down. Fixed-hyperparameter leave-one-out validation of the central NRHJSur3dq8_AA model variant against numerical relativity gives a $(2,2)$ unweighted mismatch of $1.6^{+62}_{-1.5}\times10^{-6}$ and an all-mode mismatch of $2.8^{+84}_{-2.7}\times10^{-6}$ over the full inspiral-merger-ringdown span. Sky-averaged and signal-to-noise-ratio-weighted over $32$ orientations per simulation, the model's full inspiral-merger-ringdown in-sample mismatch against the SXS numerical-relativity simulations used for training is $8.9\times10^{-7}$ to $2.8\times10^{-5}$ across total masses $40$-$120 M_\odot$. Waveforms are hybridized using post-Newtonian waveforms. Beyond accuracy, NRHJSur3dq8 provides two capabilities uncommon in numerical-relativity surrogates: nearly analytic derivatives of the strain with respect to the physical parameters, and a calibrated Gaussian-process predictive uncertainty of the model. A full non-hybridized inspiral-merger-ringdown waveform evaluates in $12.5$ ms on a single CPU call. Batched evaluation takes $0.43$ ms per waveform at a batch of $4096$, measured at a starting frequency of $25$ Hz.

papers.title: A systematic evaluation of vision-language models for observational astronomical reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly proposed as general-purpose tools for scientific data interpretation, yet their reliability on real astronomical observations across diverse modalities remains untested. We present AstroVLBench, a benchmark of over 4,100 expert-verified instances across five tasks spanning optical imaging, radio interferometry, multi-wavelength photometry, time-domain light curves, and optical spectroscopy. We systematically evaluate six state-of-the-art frontier models and find that performance is strongly modality-dependent and uncorrelated with general benchmark rankings. Mechanistic cross-model ablations reveal three concrete bottlenecks. First, prompt grounding exhibits marked model and task dependence: physical guidance yields more balanced classifications on optical imaging, whereas phenomenological prompts better navigate undersampled time-domain data. Second, presenting one-dimensional measurements as numerical tables rather than rendered plots consistently improves light-curve classification across all models by up to 23 percentage points, demonstrating that plot rendering can obscure physically relevant signal. Third, an expert audit of optical spectroscopy reveals a notable "right-answer-wrong-reason" phenomenon: across evaluated models, an average of 26% of correct predictions are accompanied by physically inconsistent or invalid reasoning chains, showing that accuracy alone is insufficient for trustworthy scientific deployment. AstroVLBench provides the first systematic, multi-modal baselines for VLMs in observational astronomy and identifies the representation, grounding, and reasoning bottlenecks that must be addressed before VLMs can be trusted as autonomous scientific interpreters.
